raw_case_text:
A 49-year-old male shepherd presented at our hospital with complaints of severe chest and back pain persisting for 6 months. He also reported a recent onset of lower limb mobility limitation over the past 2 weeks, which notably worsened at night. His fevers spiked to 39 C. His professional background involved prolonged exposure to sheep, which was particularly relevant given our initial diagnostic considerations. Upon examination, he displayed significant tenderness and percussion pain at the T9 and T10 spinous processes. His neurological assessment revealed a muscle strength of grade 2 in both lower limbs, highlighting substantial functional impairment. Initial laboratory tests indicated an elevated white blood cell count of 11.5 x 109/L with 67% neutrophils, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 10 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 9.8 mg/L, indicating the presence of inflammation. A positive result on the Rose Bengal plate agglutination test strongly suggested an infection with Brucella. Comprehensive imaging was undertaken to further evaluate the extent of the infection. Thoracic CT scans revealed considerable bone destruction and narrowing of the intervertebral spaces at T9 and T10, with local endplate destruction evident (Figures 1A-C). MRI scans demonstrated degenerative changes in the intervertebral disks and abnormal high signal changes on T2-weighted images (T2WI), indicative of an abscess compressing the spinal cord (Figures 1D-F).
Given the severity of the infection and its impact on the spinal column, we initiated an aggressive antimicrobial regimen. The patient was treated with doxycycline 200 mg daily and rifampicin 600 mg daily, supplemented with quinolones and third-generation cephalosporins, for at least 2 weeks before any surgical intervention. The surgical approach involved transforaminal-assisted posterior debridement, internal fixation, and bone graft fusion under general anesthesia. The operation was carefully documented, showing the precise placement of guide wires and the thorough debridement process using various sizes of nucleus pulposus forceps for lesion clearance (Figures 2A-I). Postoperative care included continuing the antimicrobial regimen, with added nutritional support and blood transfusions as needed. The histopathological examination with HE and Gram staining showed the extensive infiltration of inflammatory cells and confirmed Brucella infection (Figures 3A,C). Real-time PCR further confirmed the presence of Brucella melitensis DNA (Figure 3E). The patient's recovery was notable; he was provided with a waist brace and began ambulating 1 week post-surgery. At the 12-week follow-up, he reported significant relief from back pain, and his muscle strength in the lower limbs improved to grade 3. Follow-up imaging showed stable surgical repairs and proper alignment (Figure 3G).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old male shepherd presented with severe chest and back pain for 6 months and lower limb mobility limitation for 2 weeks, accompanied by fevers spiking to 39 C.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 49-year-old male shepherd presented with severe chest and back pain persisting for 6 months, along with a recent onset of lower limb mobility limitation over the past 2 weeks that notably worsened at night. His fevers spiked to 39 C.
subjective.past_medical_history: Professional background as a shepherd involving prolonged exposure to sheep. Prior chronic medical conditions, hospitalizations, prior antibiotic therapy, and allergies not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Night-worsened lower extremity weakness and mobility limitation, severe thoracic and back pain, fevers spiking to 39 C. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Spine: significant tenderness and percussion pain at the T9 and T10 spinous processes. Neurological: bilateral lower extremity muscle strength reduced to grade 2/5 (substantial functional impairment / paraparesis).
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 11.5 x 109/L (67% neutrophils); ESR: 10 mm/h; CRP: 9.8 mg/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic CT: considerable bone destruction and narrowing of the intervertebral spaces at T9 and T10, with local endplate destruction. Thoracic MRI: degenerative changes in intervertebral disks and abnormal high signal changes on T2-weighted images (T2WI), indicative of an abscess compressing the spinal cord.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellar thoracic spondylodiscitis (T9-T10) complicated by epidural abscess and compressive myelopathy/paraparesis caused by Brucella melitensis.
Confirmation: Rose Bengal plate agglutination test positive; real-time PCR of debrided tissue positive for Brucella melitensis DNA; histopathology (HE and Gram stain) demonstrating extensive infiltration of inflammatory cells and bacterial presence.
Differentials ruled out: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) and pyogenic spondylodiscitis (clinically and radiologically considered; ruled out by Brucella-specific serology, histopathology, and PCR).
Treatment & Outcome: Initiated on aggressive antimicrobial therapy with oral doxycycline 200 mg daily and oral rifampicin 600 mg daily, supplemented with quinolones and third-generation cephalosporins for at least 2 weeks preoperatively. Underwent transforaminal-assisted posterior debridement, bone graft fusion, and internal fixation under general anesthesia. Postoperatively, antimicrobial therapy was continued alongside nutritional support and blood transfusions. Fitted with a waist brace and began ambulating 1 week post-surgery. At 12-week follow-up, reported significant relief from back pain, lower limb muscle strength improved to grade 3/5, and follow-up imaging showed stable surgical repairs and proper alignment.
